title: 'A good man': Father of Belle Plaine victim speaks about son
subtitle: "I want them to remember the fun-loving spirit he had, and how he would give to anybody," said father Barry Nosal.
article: When Barry Nosal describes his son, one phrase just stands out for him.
"Everybody that knew him loved him."
It's a phrase that he feels sums up the way his son, Ryan Booker, interacted with friends, with family, with everyone in his life. He was loved, said Nosal, and it was easy to love him.

Booker, 26, was the individual at the centre of a police-involved shooting on the highway near Belle Plaine early Sunday morning, which ended fatally, according to a release from the Saskatchewan RCMP.
It's difficult for him to talk about, but Nosal wanted people to know more about his son than a handful of police-issued press releases could ever share.

"I want them to remember the fun-loving spirit he had, and how he would give to anybody," said Nosal, in an interview Monday.
"He made a mistake and this is the outcome, but he's not a monster. He's a good kid."

Booker was an outdoorsman at heart, said his father. Someone who could enjoy days away from the bustle of the city, trekking through prairie grasslands and brush during hunting season, or flicking a fish hook into a sparkling lake with high hopes for a bite.
"He loves the outdoors," said Nosal. "He could walk for miles and miles, just doing that stuff.
"Hunting and fishing were the love of his life. That, and his family," he added.

Hunting was something father and son did together, said Nosal. Booker's interest actually got him back into the sport, and Nosal said he took his son on many trips with him growing up, with friends tagging along the way.
"He was my hunting partner," said Nosal, before pausing for a deep breath.
The pair of them could spend endless hours - and dollars - during the hunting season, he went on, searching for the perfect shot on the perfect trophy buck.
"It was, 'ah, I'm not going to take that shot, but I'll come back out next week,'" he chuckled.
But Booker's life was bigger than his hobbies. He lived with his fiancé and two sons, who were a huge part of his life.
"He loved his kids," Nosal emphasized.

And he had a big passion for working on cars, said Nosal, starting at a young age. Beginning with a work experience program with a local garage in high school, Booker excelled at tinkering with engines and making cars hum.
"He was flipping motors out of cars at 16 years old, it just blows me away, because I don't have those kinds of skills."
It was a spark he built into a career he loved, and won national awards for, as a mechanic - for customers, but also for his own family anytime they needed a tune-up.
"If somebody asked him to fix their car, anyone in the family, it was, 'yup, can you come here at this time?' and it was a done deal," said Nosal. "He'd give you the shirt off his back."

Nosal said that his son's loved ones, including himself, are staying close to each other as they navigate their shock and loss. He's heard from friends and family, offering condolences for their collective loss of a son, brother, father, partner, friend and more.
Nosal said he hasn't been in contact with the police since Sunday, but didn't want to speak further on the matter at this time.
Right now, he said, the story needs to be about his son.
"I almost lived vicariously through him. I was proud of everything he did," said Nosal. "He was a good man."
